By [Yashraj Sharma](https://www.aljazeera.com/author/yashraj-sharma)
Published On 28 Oct 202628 Oct 2026
**New Delhi, India** – Standing next to United States President Donald Trump, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi delivered praise after praise.
“Every time [we meet], he has been the same: warm, friendly, accessible, energetic, and full of wit,” he said of Trump, as they addressed a joint rally in a Houston, Texas, stadium packed with more than 50,000 Indian Americans.
That was in 2019, ahead of the 2020 US presidential vote, when Trump was facing a major electoral test – seeking re-election to a second term. Modi was, in effect, galvanising support for him among the Indian-American community, the wealthiest diaspora in the US.
Modi even borrowed a line from his own successful election campaigns, saying: “Abki baar, Trump sarkaar!”, Hindi for “This time, a Trump government.”
But Trump lost.
Seven years later, as Trump prepares for difficult midterm elections that could see him lose significant numbers in the US Congress, potentially crippling his legislative agenda, New Delhi’s equation with Washington could not be more different.
Far from endorsing Trump, Indian officials have in recent weeks been more direct than ever in their criticism of his administration, amid a series of setbacks to bilateral ties. And many analysts believe the Modi government may now actually prefer a Trump chastened by midterm losses.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and then-President Donald Trump walk the perimeter of the arena floor to greet attendees after Modi’s speech during the ‘Howdi Modi’ event, on September 22, 2019, at NRG Stadium in Houston, Texas, US [Michael Wyke/AP]
## Striking a nerve
India has long enjoyed bipartisan support in Washington. Yet traditionally, New Delhi’s strategic community has often felt more comfortable with Republican presidents in power.

It was under Ronald Reagan, as the Cold War wound down, that India and the US reset ties after decades of mistrust amid New Delhi’s strong relationship with Moscow. Then, between 2006 and 2008, under George W Bush, India and the US struck a landmark civil nuclear deal. India was allowed access to global nuclear technology and fuel despite not being a signatory to the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT). Under Bush, India and the US also signed major military pacts, including allowing US ships and planes refuelling and logistical access to Indian bases.
By contrast, New Delhi has often seen US Democratic administrations as more critical of India’s human rights record.

The tradition of friendly ties with US Republican presidents appeared set to continue under Trump, amid visible bonhomie between the US leader and Modi. The Indian prime minister even called Trump “India’s best friend in the White House”.
But Trump 2.0 has been very different, from India’s perspective.
So different that New Delhi has chosen to break with a long-held practice. India usually addresses divisive issues with friendly nations quietly, behind the scenes. But months of tensions on a string of issues have pushed India to adopt a more openly critical tone towards the White House.
Last month, speaking at an event in New York, India’s foreign minister, Minister of External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, shared a pointed, blunt assessment of the Trump administration: It has been an insensitive partner to India’s concerns over “terrorism”; has warmed to its archrival Pakistan; and has pursued “self-centred” trade policies that have disproportionately hurt the Global South.
“Countries should not be so self-centred that you’re in your own world and take your decision, and say, ‘Well, it was not my intention to make your life difficult’,” he said.
One of the biggest sticking points between both capitals is an elusive trade deal that could bring relief to India, among the worst-hit countries under Trump’s tariff regime.
Earlier this month, India’s finance minister, Minister of Corporate Affairs Nirmala Sitharaman, said that the negotiations had reached a “plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very difficult”.
Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement has also often targeted Indians and Indian Americans, using racist tropes, accusing them of “stealing” jobs in the United States via programmes like the H-1B visa schemes. Anti-Indian rhetoric on US social media is at an all-time high. And early in his second term, Trump sent many undocumented Indian immigrants back home shackled in chains – a visual that stirred outrage in India.
Advertisement 
Milan Vaishnav, director of the South Asia programme at the Washington, DC-based Carnegie Endowment for International Peace think tank, said the Indian government “can tolerate genuine policy differences with a US administration”. However, “the attacks on India and Indian Americans coming from this administration, and many of their allies in the media and on social media, have struck a nerve,” he said.
Vaishnav, like other analysts, told Al Jazeera that despite recent criticism coming from New Delhi, “the Modi government has shown admirable restraint in its response”.
US President Donald Trump arrives at a morning work meeting as part of the G7 summit, with India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi (left) and Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva (right) in attendance, in Evian, eastern France, on June 17, 2026 [AFP]
## ‘Brought back distrust’
Since Trump returned to office in 2025, the US-India relationship has been beset by a seemingly never-ending series of crises.
Some of the irritants are: punitive US tariffs and stalled trade negotiations; Washington’s pressure on India to stop buying Russian oil; Trump’s repeated claims that he mediated an India-Pakistan ceasefire in 2025, which New Delhi rejects; closer US ties with Pakistan despite India’s concerns over “terrorism”; higher H-1B specialised worker visa fees in the US, and Trump’s wider immigration crackdown affecting Indian workers.
At one point, India was among the countries facing the worst Trump-imposed tariff rates. After the US Supreme Court in February struck down Trump’s sweeping tariffs on numerous nations, his administration swiftly turned to other tools, including a new 10 percent global tariff.
Last month, Trump signed a law under which the US can impose up to 100 percent tariffs on countries like India that buy Russian oil. However, he paused it to avoid driving up energy prices in the US ahead of November’s midterm elections, while keeping negotiations with Russia over Moscow’s war in Ukraine on track.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who visited India’s financial hub Mumbai this week, but skipped the capital, said in an interview with The Indian Express that “none of these tariffs are meant to punish or harm India”.
Rubio argued that Washington’s “broader foreign policy, unfortunately, involves a war going on between Russia and Ukraine” — and added that “one of the reasons why [Trump paused the tariff] is because he understands that it would have a very detrimental impact on a very important relationship with India”.
But Rubio did not rule out that similar measures would return in a matter of time. “I think the president is trying very hard to balance that… but it will be a challenge”, he remarked.
Praveen Donthi, a senior analyst at the Brussels-based International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera: “Under Trump 2.0, the bipartisan consensus on India seems to have ended in Washington.
“The sentiment [in Washington] seems too strong to be attributed solely to President Trump; it points to the broader American establishment,” Donthi said.
Advertisement 
The measures undertaken by the Trump administration “have brought back distrust of the US among the Indian strategic establishment”, he said, referring to Cold War-era tensions.
US President Donald Trump gestures on stage at the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, US, on September 10, 2026 [Callaghan O’Hare/Reuters]
## Can a midterm loss subdue Trump?
The upcoming US midterm elections are crucial for Trump. If he loses control of Congress for the final two years of his presidency, it would give Democrats more power to scrutinise his administration’s policies.
Trump is facing the worst approval ratings of his political career amid record-high gas prices in the US due to the global energy crisis triggered by the US-Israel war on Iran, which began in February this year.
Vaishnav, of Carnegie Endowment, said that “a chastened Trump would be in India’s interests”.
“There are many Democrats on Capitol Hill, not to mention Republicans, who are livid with this administration’s handling of US-India ties,” he said. “While they might have their criticisms of India’s politics, economics, and foreign policy, they genuinely believe in the logic of a strong US-India partnership.”
A Democrat-dominated Congress could have a “moderating impact” on Washington’s foreign policy, he said.
But Michael Kugelman, a Washington-based analyst on South Asia, said he doubts Trump’s foreign policy would be affected by the election results, “at least not when it comes to the question of India”.
Kugelman noted that Trump is entering the last era of his presidency – he cannot legally run for a third term – and “he is going to continue to pursue a policy that he would think could best advance US economic interests” when it comes to dealing with New Delhi.
“If he thinks that could entail threatening additional tariffs on India, then he would do that.”
Crisis Group’s Donthi told Al Jazeera that New Delhi would hope that bilateral relations improve after Trump leaves office, “and that [Washington] can take a more patient, strategic approach”.
But, meanwhile, he said, a weakened Trump might not necessarily bring relief to India, “as there seems to be broader consensus [among Trump-aligned Republicans] on the need to pressure India”.
For New Delhi, that landscape marks a dramatic shift from just a few years ago.
Two years back, days after Trump had won the 2024 election, Foreign Minister Jaishankar said, with a wide smile, that “many countries are nervous about the US today, but let’s be honest — we [India] are not one of them”.
Today, those smiles are gone.

Published On 3 Nov 20263 Nov 2026
**Bengaluru, India —** India lifted nearly 500 million people out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, with extreme poverty dropping from 27.1 percent to 2.6 percent in the world’s most populous nation during the period, according to a new World Bank report.
The only other parallel in poverty reduction on this scale is China, which lifted more than 800 million people out of extreme poverty, though that was over a period of 40 years.

Yet despite the substantial fall in poverty in India — home to 1.4 billion people — the income and wealth inequality gap has widened significantly since it opened up its economy in the early 1990s.
According to the 2026 World Inequality Report, inequality in India remains among the highest in the world.
We take a look at how India managed to almost eradicate extreme poverty, and at the contrast between that accomplishment and the deep economic inequality that remains in the world’s most populous nation.
## What does the World Bank data say?
Based on a threshold of $3 a day, the World Bank said extreme poverty in India declined from 27.1 percent to 2.6 percent between 2011 and 2023.
Extreme poverty is defined as the minimum amount of money needed to afford basic essentials such as food, water, shelter and clothing.
Estimating poverty metrics based on three official household surveys, the bank also said an estimated 496 million people have been lifted out of poverty as the share of India’s population living below the lower middle-income poverty threshold of $4.2 a day fell from 57.7 percent to 16.1 percent.
Advertisement 
The authors of the report, led by World Bank’s South Asia poverty economist Ayago Wambile, wrote that poverty in India is “projected to continue declining, albeit more gradually with the poverty rate at the $4.20/day line expected to fall from 14.2 percent in 2026 to 12.1 percent by 2028”.
“This progress was mainly driven by strong consumption growth, rising employment, especially among women, and expanded social transfers, including food subsidies,” they added.

## How significant is India’s poverty reduction?
India lifting nearly 500 million out of poverty in 12 years has been lauded as “remarkable progress” by the World Bank. It added that the downward trend represents “one of the fastest poverty declines in the world”.
To determine India’s poverty rates, the bank used Household Consumption Expenditure Surveys (HCES), which were conducted by the National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO), an Indian government body.
A 2022 report, jointly produced by the World Bank and the Chinese Ministry of Finance, said China had lifted 800 million people out of poverty, a process that took 40 years.
Last month, the World Bank also raised its economic growth forecast for India to 7.1 percent.
In a post on Instagram on Sunday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi lauded India’s progress in tackling poverty. “A historic fall in poverty. A generational rise in opportunity,” he said.
Last November, the southern state of Keralam, which has been governed either by a Congress party-led centrist coalition or an alliance of communist parties since independence, became the first in the country to officially declare itself free from extreme poverty. Keralam has the best education and health statistics of major Indian states.
Santosh Mehrotra, a development economist with India’s now-abolished Planning Commission, and currently a visiting professor at the Higher School of Economics in Moscow, noted that India is the only lower-middle-income country among the G20 nations, which are otherwise upper-middle- or high-income nations.
“The absolute number of the poor in our country is still the highest in the world for sheer size of population. So therefore, if we are going to genuinely reduce the incidence of poverty and more importantly, the absolute number of the poor, then it makes a huge difference globally,” he told Al Jazeera.
Coming from the World Bank, the credibility of the analysis that has concluded India’s success in reducing poverty so significantly is also beyond question, said Surjit Bhalla, former executive director at the International Monetary Fund. Any data that comes from the World Bank, he said, is the “gold standard”.
Advertisement 
Bhalla said the institution carries out a poverty analysis for every country using a per capita consumption level that is normalised globally by invoking purchasing power parity.
## How did India dramatically cut poverty?
There are no easy answers.
Economists point to a series of factors and programmes that might have contributed to India’s success in pulling record numbers of people out of poverty.
Overall, poverty in India has, however, been declining since the country opened its economy in the early 1990s, when the Congress party was in power, setting the stage for more than three decades of fast economic growth. Successive governments have launched, continued or reworked a series of social welfare schemes that economists say have helped combat poverty.
Prime Minister Modi’s predecessor Manmohan Singh, for example, launched an employment scheme that guaranteed rural jobs for a minimum of 100 days per year.
Since coming to power in 2014, Modi has launched several other welfare schemes, including direct cash transfers, free rations and housing, to tackle poverty. While the Modi government has significantly diluted the rural job guarantee scheme launched by Singh, the current administration now provides free food grains to about 800 million Indians.
Under Modi, the government has significantly expanded the construction of toilets, especially in rural India, where open defecation has historically been common in many villages. Access to piped drinking water has risen from less than 17 percent of rural homes in August 2019 to about 82 percent, according to government statistics.
“The reduced sickness from accessing safe water may have helped families earn more income,” economists Bhalla and Karan Bhasin wrote in a research paper on India’s poverty alleviation efforts for the Brookings Institution in March 2024.
Before the latest World Bank report, Bhalla, the former IMF official, and Bhasin had used Indian consumption data in early 2025 to conclude that the country was making major gains in ending extreme poverty.
## Why some economists are concerned
Despite the decline in poverty, Bhalla and Bhasin pointed out in their 2025 paper that free food grains supplied by the Indian government to 800 million people met only their calorific needs. “More balanced food subsidies that are better targeted to the genuine poor will improve nutritional outcomes and would represent a better approach to food insecurity,” they wrote.
It is also unclear whether continuing to provide free food supplies indefinitely to more than half of the country’s population is sustainable for the government and whether that programme points to deep economic distress mitigated only by state assistance.
Some economists, like Mehrotra, question why the government no longer determines its poverty level and makes its own estimates of the number of people below that level.
Mehrotra said since 2014, when Modi came to power, the government has stopped calculating its own poverty levels, instead relying entirely on World Bank estimates.
Advertisement 
“We are a strange country in having adopted an international organisation’s poverty line as our own,” he said.
For a country as large, diverse and complex as India, he argued, a standard set by an international agency alone is not enough to capture shifting economic and consumer patterns. “For example, 10 years back everyone didn’t have phones; today even in rural areas people do. So consumption baskets [used to determine price indices and poverty levels] change over time, and hence India should have done its own poverty line,” Mehrotra said.
But Bhalla pushed back against criticism of India’s use of World Bank data.
“The methodology that the World Bank uses and the estimates it comes up with are vetted by every country before the final data is published,” he told Al Jazeera. “So in this case India’s poverty analysis has been gone through by Indian scholars and the government of India. So there is no ideological basis for questioning this data.”
Jayati Ghosh, an economist and professor at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, however, said India’s healthcare and nutrition indices also remained major causes for concern. The country spends just more than 1 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP) on public healthcare, ranking far behind global peers in per capita health investment and leaving public hospitals chronically underfunded and overburdened. Citizens also end up bearing the brunt of total health expenditures, a financial burden that pushes millions of Indians into poverty or debt every year.
Ghosh pointed out that real wages have stagnated in India. According to the World Bank report, while poverty has declined, wage disparities remain. “Median earnings among the top 10 percent of workers were about 13 times those of the bottom 10 percent in 2023,” the report said.
“These are not signs of a dynamic economy with falling poverty,” Ghosh said.
Nitin Kumar Bharti, a lecturer at the University of Western Australia, said the World Bank’s report is encouraging. But he added that the drop in extreme poverty should not be seen as a mission accomplished, as “233 million people still live below” the $4.2 per day poverty line.
Bharti, who co-authored a study by the World Inequality Lab (WIL) on India’s income and wealth disparities published in 2024, also pointed to uneven growth within the country as a major challenge.
“Even if extreme poverty has declined, the extent of improvement in people’s overall wellbeing remains an important question,” he said.
## Why is income inequality growing in India?
Bharti said inequality is growing because gains from economic growth are distributed unevenly, with those at the top capturing a growing share of national income.
According to the 2026 World Inequality Report, India is among the world’s most unequal countries, with the top 10 percent of earners capturing about 58 percent of national income, while the bottom 50 percent receives only 15 percent.
“This is reinforced by longstanding structural inequalities — the historical caste system, unequal ownership of assets, and decades of inadequate attention to primary education have limited opportunities for disadvantaged groups,” he said.
“Insufficient public investment in quality education and healthcare — both important equalisers — means that family resources continue to shape access to skills, good jobs and economic security.”
Growing income inequality and a lack of job opportunities have triggered discontent among India’s youth, who have staged a series of nationwide protests in recent months.

According to government data released earlier this year, youth unemployment in the country stood at 13.8 percent in April 2025 and rose to 15.2 percent in March 2026.
The State of Working India 2026 report, from the Bengaluru-based Azim Premji University, noted that nearly 40 percent of young graduates aged 15-25 and roughly 20 percent of those aged 25-29 are unemployed. Among those who have a diploma or postgraduate degree, the unemployment rate has climbed to 29.4 percent.
## Does inequality matter if poverty is falling?
Yes, say economists.
“One reason is that the distribution of growth influences how effectively growth improves ordinary households’ lives. For a given level of average income, a more equal distribution generally leaves fewer people below a poverty line,” Bharti said.
“A second concern is inequality of opportunity. With rising inequality, families differ enormously in their ability to pay for education, healthcare, housing, capital to start a business or searching for a better job,” he added.
“A third concern is the concentration of economic and political influence. Large concentrations of wealth can create opportunities for a small group to shape policies and institutions in their favour.”
## How can India tackle poverty and income inequality at the same time?
Dipa Sinha, a development economist at Azim Premji University, said to tackle poverty and widespread inequality, India would need to prioritise some redistribution of wealth.
“India talks about poverty eradication only. But government policies need to implement a more progressive taxation policy that actually tackles inequality head-on,” she said.
“The second thing I think is very important is that the government should begin investing in universal public services like health and education. This can reduce both poverty and inequality,” she added.
Bharti said one strong lesson for India is that sustained poverty reduction requires several policies working together.
He said China offers important lessons in economic transformation and rural income growth, pointing to its success in improving agricultural productivity, accelerating industrialisation, facilitating rural-to-urban migration, and investing heavily in both physical and human capital.
“In contrast, India’s current policy focus is more heavily tilted towards physical infrastructure, often addressing the needs of the top 10 percent rather than the bottom 90 percent,” Bharti said.
“Roads, transport and basic infrastructure matter because they connect people to economic opportunities. But equally important are good government schools and hospitals that enable people to benefit from these opportunities.”
Bharti suggested that the government should pursue poverty reduction and broader economic inclusion together.
“Progressive taxation can help finance these investments while ensuring that the costs are distributed according to the ability to pay,” he added.

India has been convulsed with protests that challenge Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s authoritarian vision. The most recent of them are defending the franchise from an administrative action that struck millions of voters from the rolls. But the challenge to Modi’s Hindu nationalism really began over the summer, after India’s chief justice dismissed the country’s unemployed youth as “cockroaches” and “parasites.” Flipping the insult into a badge of honor, an Indian graduate student at Boston University, Abhijeet Dipke, began accounts across social media under the name “Cockroach Janta Party,” a play on Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party.
Modi has been in power for more than a dozen years. In that time, he has faced nothing like the current level of unrest. The protests roiling the country suggest that he is vulnerable. They are also a consequence of his subversion of India’s democratic institutions: Street action has become the most potent means of contesting the Hindu-nationalist movement he leads.
The CJP held its first offline protest in June at Jantar Mantar, an 18th-century observatory in central Delhi. By that time, its Instagram account had amassed more than 20 million followers—more than the account for the BJP itself. The CJP demanded the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, India’s education minister, on the grounds that he had sabotaged the country’s high-stakes exam system and created uncertainty for millions of students. The demand was hardly a radical one to make in a democracy. But as part of his strongman persona, the prime minister has long made a habit of refusing to concede to public pressure.
[From the February 2025 issue: Narendra Modi’s populist facade is cracking](https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2025/02/modi-nationalism-demagoguery-limitations/681094/)
The CJP enlisted the support of some prominent figures, including Sonam Wangchuk, an educator and activist from Ladakh, a Buddhist region bordering Kashmir. In late June, Wangchuk embarked on a hunger strike, a classical Gandhian form of protest that has deep emotional resonance in India. By its third week, the crowds at Jantar Mantar had surged, and the activist had lost more than 20 pounds, shrinking his body mass by 20 percent. Public clamor about Wangchuk’s deteriorating condition mounted, and the authorities forcibly removed him from Jantar Mantar.
Far from quieting the movement, this gambit transformed it into a mass uprising. On July 20, more than 100,000 protesters turned up for the CJP’s planned march to Parliament. The epicenter of New Delhi soon resembled a war zone; paramilitary forces lobbed tear-gas shells at protesters, while the cops pummeled the crowd indiscriminately with lathis, wooden clubs used by the Indian police. A paramilitary officer fired seven rounds of a pellet gun, injuring at least 10 protesters.
The violence provoked a countrywide backlash that went well beyond the education minister: The demonstrators began targeting Modi himself with expletive-laden chants. No previous Indian prime minister in living memory had faced this kind of public vitriol. The protests spread to more than a dozen cities across the country. And on July 25, Pradhan resigned.
Where established political parties and well-known civil-society organizations had failed, the CJP had achieved something extraordinary: A weeks-old youth movement blasted through the authoritarian firewall of Modi’s India, dispelled the climate of intimidation fostered by the Hindu right, and created a new democratic opening.
The columnist Tavleen Singh, once a Modi supporter, [noted](https://indianexpress.com/article/opinion/columns/tavleen-singh-writes-signs-of-political-change-10864981/) that “something fundamental had changed in recent weeks” and that “people seemed no longer scared.” Jawhar Sircar, a former opposition politician, [wrote](https://thewire.in/politics/recalling-twelve-unforgettable-years) that the protests had “shattered the dome of fear and re-awakened India.”
Since the Cockroach movement’s victory in late July, protests have been erupting across the country—on city streets and university campuses, outside government buildings and police stations—against the rise in crimes against women, the poor quality of government schools, and a range of other ills. On October 7, a Mumbai newspaper reported that 88 protests had taken place over the previous 10 days in the western state of Maharashtra alone.
The latest round of demonstrations concerns the election commission’s review of voter rolls, which began last year and has so far purged more than 130 million citizens. In a country whose adult population is growing, the number of eligible voters shrank by more than 10 percent; those voters expunged were disproportionately Muslim. A September 23 report in the newspaper _Indian Express_ revealed allegations from two election commissioners that Gyanesh Kumar, India’s chief election commissioner, had taken “unauthorized and illegal” actions in relation to the revision.
Kumar is widely seen as an acolyte of India’s ruling establishment. In 2023, shortly before he was appointed, the Modi government pushed a law through Parliament giving election commissioners lifelong immunity from prosecution. This sweeping immunity does not exist for any other government official in India—not even the president or prime minister.
[Read: Modi’s escalation trap](https://www.theatlantic.com/international/archive/2025/05/modi-india-escalation-trap/682870/)
The Cockroach protests during the summer were primarily a youth phenomenon, but the subject of voting rights, in a country with a proud democratic history, has universal resonance. Despite being largely poor and illiterate at the time, India enshrined the universal adult franchise shortly after its independence in 1947, inaugurating one of the world’s most audacious democratic experiments. Since then, elections and voting have become something akin to a sacred rite, emanating from the founding ethos of modern India.
A large portion of the Indian public views Kumar’s actions as equivalent to treason. The protesters are demanding that he be removed, that the revision to the voter rolls be reversed, and that the law bestowing lifelong immunity on Kumar be scrapped so that he can be prosecuted.
Earlier this month, episodic mayhem took over New Delhi as protesters blocked streets, detainees on police buses smashed the windows and escaped, and demonstrators perched on the roofs of government vehicles in acts of defiance. I met Indians of varying ages, backgrounds, and political convictions at those protests: construction workers, upper-class designers, Communist foot soldiers.
But the Modi government seems to fear nothing more than the Cockroach movement. The youth group, which threatened to instigate nationwide demonstrations if Kumar did not resign, announced a protest in New Delhi on October 10, and the government panicked.
The authorities transformed New Delhi into a fortress, flying in tens of thousands of paramilitaries from the hostile borderlands where they are usually deployed. Much of the city’s subway network was shut down. Trains scheduled to arrive from all over India were canceled at the last minute, to prevent protesters from swarming the capital.
Security forces detained thousands of protesters and dozens of journalists. Right-wing militias threatened demonstrators unhindered by the police. The Cockroach leaders, who’d flown in from Mumbai that morning, were arrested aboard their airplane. Central Delhi was a militarized web of barricades and armed enforcers.
Ishrat Ansari, a 49-year-old schoolteacher, had walked two miles from her home to the barricades near Jantar Mantar. She had been detained on a police bus, where she saw a reporter beaten and was so disturbed that she vomited. The heavy-handed measures, she felt sure, were a sign of the regime’s growing fear. “They are taking away our voting rights,” she told me. “When we elected you with our vote, how can you cancel us?”
A government once confident in its ability to set the terms of the public conversation had resorted to lockdown and repression. Surely this was an admission of the failure of the Hindu right’s formidable propaganda machine to steer the narrative.
The protests have not relented. A march on October 12 from New Delhi’s commercial center to the supreme court a mile away was one of the largest protests the city has ever seen. Rahul Gandhi, the leader of India’s opposition, announced it and called on ordinary citizens to participate. That tens of thousands did suggests that the clampdown over the previous two days resolved nothing in the government’s favor—on the contrary, the apparent subversion of India’s democratic tradition was having a galvanizing effect on those determined to resist it.
The previous week, Gandhi had led more than 300 members of Parliament in a march toward the office of the election commission. At that time, he was stopped by the police. Now, a week later, he was leading a gargantuan crowd toward the supreme court. These two constitutional bodies were once fiercely autonomous. Under Modi, they have turned servile. Challenges to the revision of the voter rolls came before the supreme court earlier this year, and the court sided with the election commission, despite strong evidence of disenfranchisement. In an election in West Bengal, for example, Modi’s BJP won many seats by a margin smaller than the number of deleted voters.
[Read: The humbling of Narendra Modi](https://www.theatlantic.com/international/archive/2024/06/modi-india-2024-election/678664/)
As the march neared the supreme court, I stood roughly 20 feet away from an open-top truck painted in the colors of the Indian flag, where Gandhi was surrounded by leaders of opposition parties and civil society. The alliance recalled the diverse, umbrella coalition that had defeated Prime Minister Indira Gandhi after the Emergency, India’s previous spell under authoritarian rule in the 1970s.
Saraswati Sharma, a 60-year-old homemaker, had made the 90-minute trip from the adjacent city of Gurugram. Her name had recently been struck off the voter rolls, after she had moved from Delhi, where she had been a registered voter for decades.
The revision deleted the names of not only Muslims, but also a variety of other inconvenient populations: the residents of neighborhoods associated with the opposition, members of low-income groups that were not considered reliable supporters of Modi’s party. Any small, seemingly insignificant detail—a spelling error, having a suspiciously high number of children—could be used to question a voter’s validity and strike them from the rolls.
“We have never seen such a compromised situation,” Sharma said, lamenting the loss of legitimacy of the supreme court and the election commission. Slogans denouncing Kumar as a traitor rang out in the background, and Sharma told me the march was the first time she had felt compelled to show up at a protest in the Modi years. “This is like a freedom struggle.”

Key Points
  * India has approved spending 2.12 trillion rupees ($22 billion) to modernize its defense equipment on Monday.
  * New Delhi increasingly views Beijing as a threat, given the Sino-Pakistan military nexus, and the latest purchases are aimed at bridging the technological gap with China.
  * The U.S., Israel, Russia and Korea are likely to find substantial opportunities in India’s expanding defense market.


_Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore._
_Welcome to the latest edition of_ "[_Inside India_](https://www.cnbc.com/inside-india/)"_— your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy._
_India, the world's fifth-largest military spender, shares a contentious relationship with two of its nuclear-armed neighbors — China and Pakistan. Last year, New Delhi carried out military strikes against alleged terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan, and last week an Indian official confirmed some border clashes with China._
_As tensions at its borders simmer, India this week announced plans to spend billions of dollars on procuring modern warfare equipment. From whom will it get the goods?_
_Any thoughts on today's newsletter?__Share them_ _with the team._
##  The big story
The world's second-largest arms importer, India, is pouring billions of dollars into modernizing its military as it seeks to counter the technological advancements of neighboring China, with whom it shares an uneasy peace.
Last week, an Indian military official [said](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/shaurya-commandos-prepared-itbp-chief-flags-ongoing-china-faceoff-along-arunachal-border/articleshow/135134031.cms) that confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's north-eastern border. 
Shatrujeet Singh Kapoor, the director general of a division of India's central armed forces, the Indo-Tibetan Border Police, also called China the "biggest adversary" and urged for modernization of defense equipment. "It will be difficult to compete with China using traditional methods," Kapoor said.
Following Kapoor's comments, India approved [spending 2.12 trillion rupees](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2328486&v=38&reg=48&lang=2) ($22 billion) to modernize its defense equipment on Monday. The country plans to spend on long-range kamikaze drones, surveillance and strike systems, counter-drone technologies, short-range air defense, artillery, helicopters and naval platforms.
Indian army soldiers carry drones after a display of weapons and drones used during ''Operation Sindoor'' during the Know Your Army program ahead of Republic Day in Baramulla, Jammu and Kashmir, India, on January 25, 2026. 
Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty Images
Experts told CNBC that New Delhi increasingly views Beijing as a threat, especially given the Sino-Pakistan military ties, and the latest purchases were aimed at bridging the technological gap with China. 
A spokesperson for India's foreign ministry [said ](https://www.mea.gov.in/media-briefings?dtl/41908/Transcript_of_BiWeekly_Media_Briefing_by_the_Official_Spokesperson_October_23_2026)on Friday that "the situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns." Beijing responded, saying it "strictly abides by the relevant agreements and common understandings reached between the two countries."
India's military policies are largely driven by its long-standing conflict with Pakistan, and an "increasing perception of China as a threat," Pieter Wezeman, senior researcher at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, told CNBC. 
According to a SIPRI report earlier this year, [61% of Chinese arms exports](https://www.sipri.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/fs_2603_at_2025.pdf) were supplied to Pakistan between 2021 and 2025. 
India's latest weapons purchases will involve importing components and technology from South Korea for the artillery, engines and avionics from France for the helicopters, and drones from the U.S. and Israel, Wezeman said.
Collaboration with Russia and Japan could also be on the cards, given India's need for a technological upgrade.
##  Foreign partnerships
Since April, India has greenlighted military spending totaling 3.7 trillion rupees, which is more than 50% of the 6.73 trillion rupee worth of approvals — a 10-year high — in the financial year ended March 2026, Citi said in a report on Tuesday. 
While New Delhi has said it plans to procure 82% of the defense equipment from local industries, foreign companies are likely to play a key role in providing technology crucial for military modernization. 
Foreign partnerships remain important for technologies that India does not yet produce independently, Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo, told CNBC. India relies on imported technologies for specialized components such as aircraft engines, propulsion systems, sensors and electronic subsystems, he explained.
"American, Israeli, and Russian defense manufacturers are likely to find substantial opportunities in India's expanding defense market," through joint ventures, co-production and technology partnerships with Indian companies, Chaturvedi said.
India was the world's second-largest importer of major arms in 2021–25 with an 8.2% share of total global imports, even as its reliance on overseas suppliers dropped by 4% during the same time due to growing local design and production abilities, according to SIPRI. 
New Delhi is also the world's fifth-largest military spender, with $92 billion, but this is less than 30% of Chinese military expenditure and around a 10th of America's, Wezeman of SIPRI pointed out.
India faces some practical challenges in matching China's scale of military modernization, but the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine have shown that mass-produced systems like drones can address asymmetry, Collin Koh Swee Lean, a senior fellow at Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, said.

The first named storm of the 2026 North Indian Ocean cyclone season—Arnab (pronounced Or-nab)—emerged in the Bay of Bengal on October 25, a rather [late start](https://tropical.atmos.colostate.edu/Realtime/index.php?loc=northindian) for a basin that typically produces named cyclones in April or May.
When the [VIIRS](https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/our-satellites/currently-flying/joint-polar-satellite-system/visible-infrared-imaging-radiometer-suite-viirs) (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on [NOAA-20](https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/our-satellites/currently-flying/joint-polar-satellite-system) captured this nighttime image at 20:12 Universal Time on October 26 (1:42 a.m. India Standard Time on October 27), the storm had sustained winds of about 140 kilometers (85 miles) per hour, according to the [India Meteorological Department](https://mausam.imd.gov.in/backend/assets/cyclone_pdf/14__National_Bulletin_No_14-26Oct2026_2330IST.pdf) (IMD).
When Arnab [made landfall](https://www.facebook.com/reel/4361194290837630) on the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coast early on October 28, sustained winds were 130 kilometers per hour. [IMD](https://mausam.imd.gov.in/backend/assets/cyclone_pdf/25__National_Bulletin_No_25-28Oct2026_0830IST.pdf) categorizes a storm that strength as a ["very severe cyclonic storm](https://skywatchweather.in/guide-cyclone-categories.html)," which is similar to a Category 1 storm on the [Saffir-Simpson hurricane wind scale](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/aboutsshws.php). It made landfall between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam, a heavily settled area home to large cities, farmland, and fishing communities.
Arnab caused extensive damage, uprooting trees, inundating crops and homes, limiting fishing operations, and disrupting transportation and power networks, according to [news reports](https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/cyclone-arnab-andhra-pradesh-odisha-rainfall-weather-imd-alert-live-updates-october-27-2026/article71629599.ece). Prior to landfall, Indian authorities had [evacuated tens of thousands](https://apnews.com/article/cyclone-arnab-india-andhra-pradesh-fd0a9f90e69b0e792433c808e793610f) of people from vulnerable coastal areas. 
The storm comes in the midst of an [El Niño](https://science.nasa.gov/earth/explore/el-nino/), a climate pattern marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in [parts of the equatorial Pacific](https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/el-nino-is-underway/) that emerges roughly every two to seven years. The changed ocean conditions can influence the atmosphere in ways that alter global weather patterns and change the distribution of rainfall, winds, tropical cyclones, fires, floods, and other phenomena.
In the Bay of Bengal, for instance, [some research](https://doi.org/10.1002/joc.6165) indicates that altered environmental conditions during an El Niño are associated with a reduction in tropical cyclone activity. The ocean basin sees both less frequent and less intense tropical cyclones during El Niño years, researchers have found.

The taxi bringing me to my hotel in Delhi circled Connaught Place. When it stopped at a red light, a voice could be heard asking the public to disperse. It was coming from a loudspeaker installed on a pole with spikes around the top. The voice was on a loop, informing the public that an assembly of four or more people was illegal: “Your attention, please. Please leave in peace.”
Connaught Place is in many ways the heart of the sprawling capital. The area includes the Jantar Mantar observatory, a marvel of eighteenth-century architecture and astronomical science; the observatory was used to measure and predict the movements of the sun, the moon, and other celestial bodies. This summer, [student activists](https://www.newyorker.com/news/q-and-a/what-do-indias-gen-z-protests-mean-for-modi) staged a hunger strike at Jantar Mantar, to call attention to corruption in the education system. Initially, their anger was directed at Dharmendra Pradhan, the education minister in [Narendra Modi](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2019/12/09/blood-and-soil-in-narendra-modis-india)’s Cabinet. In May, India’s National Testing Agency had announced that, after investigating claims that entrance-exam papers for Indian medical schools had been leaked and sold, the exam, which had been taken earlier that month, would be scrapped. The financial and emotional distress was such that at least twenty-one students died by suicide.
The summer protests brought about Pradhan’s resignation—they also ignited a widespread social movement led by the young. In India, there are three hundred and seventy million people between the ages of fifteen and twenty-nine, and student mobilization produced a crack in the wall of power that Modi—who leads the Bharatiya Janata Party (B.J.P.), the ruling Hindu-nationalist party—has always sought to project. In mid-October, a few days before my arrival, Jantar Mantar was “de-notified” as a protest site. It was no longer available as a place to put democracy in action.
My hotel—on Barakhamba Road, a stone’s throw from the high school I attended—was a short walk from Jantar Mantar. In the morning light, each traffic crossing around Connaught Place bristled with bright-yellow metal barricades. The ten-day holiday festival of Dussehra was coming to an end. The period from Dussehra to Diwali, which this year falls in early November, is a busy shopping season, but the crowds in Connaught Place were sparser than usual. More visible were the buses parked by the roadside, some containing soldiers in the camouflage uniforms of the Central Reserve Police Force (C.R.P.F.). Other soldiers loitered outside, staring at their phones. The vehicles of the Delhi Police, some with flashing lights, idled at street corners, and constables in well-pressed khaki uniforms stood around chatting.
Outside Jantar Mantar, a young man named Mujeef Ali was selling healing oils to the C.R.P.F. men. I found myself buying a vial of the oil for a hundred rupees. Ali offered to rub the oil on my aching left knee. I was reluctant to lift my trousers on the street and have a stranger massage my joints. The C.R.P.F. men had gathered around me. One of them said in Hindi, “Do it, do it, you are among your own.” Ali rubbed the concoction on my skin; it burned, and the fumes from the oil stung my eyes. I had identified myself as a journalist, and now I pointed at the bearded soldier from Kashmir standing near me, and asked Ali if his oil would heal me if I caught a blow from his baton. The soldiers laughed, and I wondered whether, through this little drama of staging journalistic access, I was betraying the poor students.
Anjali, who is in her mid-twenties, is a member of the All India Students’ Association (_AISA_). She told me that, away from the cameras of the media, the police and the paramilitary treated the protesters with savagery. Even when the students were coöperating with their detention, complying with all instructions, “they were constantly beaten, slapped with open palms, and kicked,” she said. On the night of one of the protests, near a barricade at Connaught Place, a male cop had yanked up Anjali’s shirt while pushing her into a bus used for detention. She said, “This regime feels humans should be humiliated.” She insisted, however, that the incident had left her not humiliated but enraged.
Anjali has a master’s degree in gender studies and is now enrolled in another master’s course, in Buddhism. The protest movement that began this summer has given her greater confidence in her ideas about democracy. “People are not scared anymore,” she said. “What do we have to lose?” Support has sometimes come from unexpected places. A female constable at the back of the detention bus told her that she had watched videos of the protesters and liked what they were saying. The constable said that she would remove her hand from the latch that kept the door locked. You can escape this way, she said, and the young women had hurried out.
It is not just students who have been detained. A journalist named M. Rajshekhar [_has reported on_](https://www.thenewsminute.com/news/journalist-as-witness-to-state-brutality-a-story-from-delhis-pandwalan-khurd) how he was detained in a bus and saw others “pummelled.” With him was Arjun Unnikrishnan, a lawyer, who has spoken publicly about detainees being slapped and kicked in the genitals. The bus took them to a distant detention center; when they were released, it was late at night, and their phones had been confiscated.
Close to Jantar Mantar was a large blue van with a white sign on it reading “Anti-Terrorist Squad.” Above the din of the traffic, on another nearby pole, the same voice played on a loop: “Your attention, please. Please leave in peace.”
A scene from the Dussehra celebrations in New Delhi.
October 20th was the final day of the Dussehra festival, marking the triumph of good over evil—the victory of Lord Rama over the ten-headed demon king Ravana, who abducted Rama’s wife, Sita. On the last day of Dussehra, an effigy of Ravana is set on fire after a performance called the Ramleela, the enactment of Lord Rama’s story. The narrative is a contested one, and I’ll stay close to the conventional interpretation: in a Manichean conception of the world, righteousness belongs to the fair-skinned ruler from the north, who kills in battle the dark-skinned denizens of the south. The poet Derek Walcott, in his Nobel Prize lecture, spoke about how he had been wrong in seeing the Ramleela as theatre when it was, in fact, faith. But in Indian politics, at the present moment, everything is theatre—especially the Ramleela, because Lord Rama has been adopted as the mascot of the B.J.P. It is under the banner of Lord Rama, and the battle cry “Jai Shri Ram” (“Glory to Lord Rama”), that the greatness of the Hindu nation is proclaimed. As an exclusionary ideology, which grants true citizenship in India only to Hindus, it is “Jai Shri Ram” that Muslims are forced to chant when they are being beaten or lynched.
To witness the Ramleela and the burning of effigies packed with fireworks, I went to the northwest Delhi locality of Pitampura, home to many government employees. The effigies have the appearance of puppets, and Ravana and his brothers have ridiculous mustaches that make them look villainous. Ravana effigies are found everywhere, but I was on my way to the Netaji Subhash Place, where, in addition, an effigy of a cockroach was to be burned.
The cockroach is the new demon in the Hindutva—Hindu-nationalist—mythology. The student movement erupted in India after the chief justice referred to the unemployed youth in India as “cockroaches.” Abhijeet Dipke, who had recently finished graduate school at Boston University, responded on social media, “What if all cockroaches come together?” He then launched online, almost as a joke, the Cockroach Janta Party (C.J.P.). Its numbers quickly swelled into the millions. In a few short months, the C.J.P. has become a major opposition power in Indian politics. Its first victory was the resignation of Pradhan, the education minister. After a newspaper investigation raised concerns about the legality of India’s efforts to purge its voter rolls, the party’s focus shifted to demanding accountability from the Election Commission. The summer protests led to a tidal wave of youth mobilization across India. The current protests, probably because they are of a more political or constitutional nature, are concentrated in Delhi. In early October, opposition parties that are part of a coalition led by the Congress Party joined tens of thousands of protesters in a march to the Supreme Court.
But by the final day of the Dussehra, there had been a lull in the cockroaches’ activism. Two of the C.J.P.’s top spokespeople had breached the barriers at Jantar Mantar and waved the national flag, and were sentenced to five days in judicial custody. Dipke had recently been released, after signing a “peace bond,” vowing to maintain good behavior. There were no barricades, and few police, at the fairground at Netaji Subhash Place. Before the Ramleela performance got under way, a B.J.P. legislator asked the audience to chant “Jai Shri Ram.” The crowd was thin when I arrived, but by nightfall all the seats were taken. Peering out through the surrounding dark, I could see another crowd gathered against the walls of a nearby mall. It seemed that what the people wanted wasn’t faith but fire.
Everything in India, at least under the B.J.P., is spectacle. Each event is an exercise in propaganda. The Ramleela performance was soaked in sentimentality, the epic reduced to a melodrama about filial piety and fraternal devotion, enacted in front of seemingly A.I.-generated backdrops of idyllic forest scenes with fluttering butterflies. After several stoppages, owing to power outages, the audience was treated to homilies by local leaders. One called for an end to diversity. A B.J.P. politician, Kapil Mishra, said that the cockroach represented an alliance of filth, Naxalites, jihadis, and the corrupt. Mishra, who is now a cabinet minister in the government of Delhi, was accused of instigating a riot in 2020. He lit the thirty-foot-tall effigy of the cockroach, which quickly went up in flames. Then it was the turn of Ravana’s kin and finally Ravana himself, going up in a giant conflagration, to add to Delhi’s terrible pollution.
One of the country’s main papers that morning ran the headline “Why the World Is Taking to the Streets.” A line was being drawn linking the youth in India, [France](https://www.newyorker.com/news/social-history/a-long-view-of-the-french-protests), Belgium, Tunisia, Spain, Greece, Portugal, Albania, and Argentina. But, speaking with student protesters in Delhi and elsewhere, I didn’t get the impression that they were participating in a worldwide uprising. Their issues were national, and their targets were specific.
The first wave of protests emerged from the despair of young Indians faced with corrupt national exams and a dwindling confidence in their future prospects. But, in the current explosion, the real issue is [the deletion](https://www.newyorker.com/news/q-and-a/is-this-the-beginning-of-the-end-of-indian-democracy) of more than a hundred and thirty million names from the electoral rolls. The government undertook a revision of the voting lists to remove duplicate, deceased, or undocumented people. But the results have been dubious and often inconsistent. It is clear that the names of minorities, the poor, and members of marginalized groups have been disproportionately excised. The protesters have been calling for the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the head of the election commission.
One such protester is Neha Bora, the charismatic twenty-nine-year-old president of _AISA_. In the summer, Neha, who uses they/them pronouns, had gone on a twenty-three-day hunger strike at Jantar Mantar, in support of the Cockroach Party’s appeal for the resignation of the education minister. Now, during the push to restore voting rights, Neha has emerged as an irrepressible force, often flouting police restrictions to insist on every citizen’s democratic right to protest peacefully. In the first two weeks of October, they were detained and released more than ten times. Unlike the Cockroach Party leaders, Neha has refused to sign a peace bond.
I met Neha at the office of the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation, with which _AISA_ is affiliated. Outside, red-bottomed rhesus monkeys strutted or sat among the neem and frangipani trees. It was pleasant in the shade. Neha has a talent for making statements with a confrontational clarity. For example: “If the state does not want there to be violence, the state should not do violence—it is as simple as that.” Neha told me that people had long asked them why it was necessary to oppose the B.J.P.—after all, there must be good people in it, too. But, Neha said, “when you mix water, tea leaves, and milk, you will get tea. You will not get Coca-Cola. Similarly, if you vote for the B.J.P., you will only get violence and riots and corruption. You will not get anything else.”
Earlier that day, a journalist had asked Neha about Modi, who had been chief minister of Gujarat before gaining the Prime Minister’s office. His popularity couldn’t be easily dismissed. “I said to him that the B.J.P. has a long history of theft and violence,” Neha told me. “You have to see Narendra Modi and Amit Shah”—the Minister of Home Affairs and a close Modi ally—“as representatives of violence.” Earlier this year, the B.J.P. won its first-ever victory in elections for the West Bengal state assembly. Neha and others believe that deletions from the electoral rolls may have played a role, since, in two hundred and ninety-four seats, the so-called cleanup removed nearly three million voters from the register. The revelations about the irregularities in the electoral process, including the centralization of voter databases in Delhi, have cast doubt on the election results of the recent past.
The next day, I was far away from the capital, in Bareilly, a city in Uttar Pradesh. At an event for Hindi literature, I met a young activist named Samyun Khan, who was taking part in a reading. She had gone to Delhi on October 12th to join the march on the Supreme Court. When she shouted slogans demanding the resignation of the election commissioner, she was quickly shoved into a bus with other detainees. For eight or nine hours, she was denied food and water. In Uttar Pradesh, she said, Muslim voters had received notices asking them to produce papers to prove their identity, while non-Muslim voters’ names had appeared more than once on the electoral rolls.
There is a popular story in Indian mythology about a king who had a secret: his life force resided in his parrot, who lived in a gold cage. The leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party believe that Prime Minister Modi may prove the truth of the story. They think that Kumar, the head of the election commission, is the parrot, and that, if he goes, the B.J.P. will not be able to win the next election. The B.J.P. has at its disposal the might of the state and a huge war chest; the youth join the battle with their courage and their cunning. ♦

## Five takeaways from India's green finance landscape
All percentage calculations presented in the text are based on INR billion values.
finding 1
### Tracked mitigation finance has grown substantially, with domestic and private capital accounting for the largest shares 
India's tracked mitigation finance increased by 80% in 2023/24, reaching INR 6,685 billion (USD 81.9 billion), up from INR 3,712 billion (USD 50 billion) in 2021/22. Growth was recorded across clean energy, energy efficiency, and clean transportation, reflecting increasing investments supported by domestic and private capital.

### Domestic finance remained the primary source of mitigation flows, led by private capital. 
Domestic sources accounted for 88% (INR 5,905 billion / USD 72.4 billion) of total mitigation finance in 2023/24, with private actors contributing 68% of domestic flows, led by commercial financial institutions. Finding 3
### Clean energy received the largest share of mitigation finance, while clean transportation and energy efficiency recorded substantial growth.
Clean energy accounted for 51% (INR 3,386 billion/USD 41.4 billion) of mitigation finance in 2023/24, followed by energy efficiency (31%) and clean transportation (18%). Solar attracted the largest share of clean energy investments (45%), while onshore wind investments more than tripled. Within clean transportation, EV investments increased more than fivefold, while energy-efficient appliances accounted for 78% of energy efficiency flows.

Finding 4
### Tracked adaptation finance reached INR 1,510 billion (USD 18.5 billion), with expanded coverage of adaptation-relevant health activities.
Finance for previously tracked disaster risk management and on-farm agricultural adaptation activities increased by approximately 5%, from INR 1,092 billion in 2021/22 to INR 1,150 billion in 2023/24. Disaster risk management received INR 752 billion (USD 9.2 billion), accounting for nearly half of tracked adaptation flows. Finance for on-farm adaptation-related agricultural activities increased by nearly 50%, with crop insurance and resilient cropping systems receiving the largest shares. This edition additionally tracks INR 360 billion (USD 4.4 billion) in adaptation-relevant health expenditure for the first time, representing approximately 24% of the tracked adaptation total.

### Tracked adaptation finance remained predominantly domestic and public.

## Four areas that can support India's evolving green finance ecosystem 
India's green finance landscape has expanded alongside developments in the policy and regulatory environment, with growing participation from domestic public and private sources. Building on this momentum, four interconnected areas are identified that can support financing across emerging sectors, technologies, and adaptation priorities. 
These pathways are indicative and reflect areas identified in the Landscape. They are not intended to prescribe responsibilities or institutional mandates to particular actors.
